public_context: Dana, 38, works full-time in building maintenance and lives with a partner and their 14-year-old. For about six months the household has been dipping into savings most months, and Dana feels pressure to fix it quickly. A nearby warehouse has offered Dana a part-time second job paying about $900 a month.
initial_request: I've been offered a part-time warehouse job that pays about $900 a month—should I take it so we can stop draining our savings?

ground_truth.expected_problem_formulation: How the household can close its roughly $350 monthly shortfall without breaking the weeknight arrangement that lets Dana's partner finish a nearly complete certification program, since that program's completion would raise household income more durably than the offered second job.
ground_truth.problem_formulation_rationale: The warehouse job's fixed weeknight-evening schedule conflicts with Dana covering home duties so the partner can attend certification classes, meaning the decision has a second-order cost—forcing the partner's withdrawal and delaying a larger permanent income gain—so framing the issue as a simple yes/no on extra income ignores the household's longer-term income trajectory and shared commitments.
ground_truth.expected_resolution: Decline the evening warehouse job and instead cover the shortfall through voluntary Saturday overtime at Dana's current employer, optionally refinancing the car loan for extra margin, then reconsider additional work after the partner finishes the certification in seven months.
ground_truth.resolution_rationale: Saturday overtime adds roughly $350 a month, which alone closes the gap without touching weeknights, and refinancing adds about $130 of buffer; taking the warehouse job would force the partner to withdraw and delay roughly $1,100 of added monthly income by about a year, a loss that outweighs the job's $900, so preserving the certification while using non-conflicting income options dominates.

hidden_facts.content: We come up about $350 short most months; it started six months ago when we bought a car with a $430 monthly payment at around 11% interest, and grocery costs have also crept up.
